summary: Specifies an EAP mechanism for authentication and session key distribution using the Authentication and Key Agreement mechanism used in UMTS and CDMA2000 mobile networks. AKA uses symmetric keys, typically on a subscriber identity module. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Your phone's SIM card shares a secret with your carrier. This memo lets that secret be used to log in to other networks, without sending the secret itself.

questions: how does eap-aka authenticate a sim card
what is fast re-authentication in eap-aka
subtitle: How a SIM card's secret can log a device into any network that speaks EAP, with mutual authentication.

tldr.problem: Mobile operators already authenticate subscribers with the 3rd generation AKA mechanism, but other networks that use EAP, such as wireless LANs, had no standard way to reuse it.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-AKA carries the AKA challenge and response inside EAP messages as attributes. The server gets an authentication vector, the peer proves itself with its identity module, and both derive session keys, with optional identity privacy and fast re-authentication.
tldr.outcome: Any technology that can use EAP can rely on the existing mobile authentication infrastructure. The RFC is Informational and has been updated by RFC 5448 and RFC 9048.

today: RFC 4187 is an Informational document that has been updated by RFC 5448, which adds the EAP-AKA' variant and bidding down protection, and by RFC 9048, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Why EAP-AKA Exists
sections.content:
EAP-AKA is an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method that uses the 3rd generation Authentication and Key Agreement (AKA) mechanism from UMTS and CDMA2000. AKA is based on challenge-response and symmetric cryptography, and typically runs in a UMTS Subscriber Identity Module (USIM) or a CDMA2000 (R)UIM. Compared with 2nd generation mechanisms such as GSM, it provides substantially longer keys and mutual authentication.

Putting AKA inside EAP allows new uses: a secure PPP authentication method for devices that already contain an identity module, use of the mobile authentication infrastructure for wireless LANs, and a seamless way to rely on AKA with any other technology that can use EAP.

An IESG note says the protocol was developed by 3GPP and published for information. The EAP working group verified compatibility with EAP, but no other review was done, including validation of the security claims or the underlying UMTS AKA algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone companies already have a way to check your SIM card. This memo lets other kinds of networks use that same check, so one card can open many doors.

sections.title: How a Full Authentication Works
sections.content:
The SIM and the home operator's network share a secret key beforehand. To authenticate, the home environment builds an authentication vector from the key and a sequence number: a random part RAND, an authenticator AUTN that proves the network to the identity module, an expected result XRES, and a 128-bit integrity key IK and 128-bit encryption key CK. RAND and AUTN are 128 bits each.

After an optional identity exchange, the EAP server obtains a vector, perhaps from the operator's Authentication Centre (AuC), and sends an EAP-Request/AKA-Challenge with AT_RAND, AT_AUTN and AT_MAC. The peer runs the AKA algorithm, verifies AUTN (so it knows the server is legitimate) and replies with AT_RES and AT_MAC. If both are correct the server sends EAP-Success. At minimum this takes two round trips. Vectors may be stored for later but may not be reused.

If the sequence number in AUTN is out of range, the peer sends an AKA-Synchronization-Failure message carrying AT_AUTS (112 bits). The server resynchronizes and sends a new challenge.
sections.plainLanguage: The network asks a secret question that only the real card can answer, and the card also checks that the question came from its real network. If both pass, they are in.

sections.title: Identities and Privacy
sections.content:
Subscribers are identified by an IMSI, a string of not more than 15 digits, while AAA protocols use a Network Access Identifier (NAI) of the form username@realm. EAP-AKA uses three kinds of username:

  • Permanent, which SHOULD be derived from the IMSI as the digit 0 followed by the IMSI.
  • Pseudonym, a temporary identity issued by the server.
  • Fast re-authentication, a one-time identity the peer MUST NOT reuse.

The first two are used only on full authentication, the last only on fast re-authentication.

Optional identity privacy hides the permanent identity from eavesdroppers, because a fixed identity would let observers track the user. The server sends pseudonyms and fast re-authentication identities encrypted in the AT_ENCR_DATA attribute. The RFC notes that a peer with no pseudonym yet must send its permanent identity in the clear, and that an active attacker impersonating the network can use AT_PERMANENT_ID_REQ to ask for the IMSI.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of always shouting your real name, the network gives you a nickname that changes. Only the network knows who the nickname belongs to, so strangers cannot follow you around.

sections.title: Fast Re-Authentication
sections.content:
Full authentication needs fresh vectors from the AuC, which is costly when done often. EAP-AKA therefore offers an optional, cheaper fast re-authentication that does not use the AKA algorithms. It reuses the K_aut and K_encr keys from the preceding full authentication and derives a fresh Master Session Key from the original Master Key.

An unsigned 16-bit counter in AT_COUNTER limits the number of successive re-authentications, contributes to the keying material and protects against replays. Both sides set it to one on full authentication, and on each later fast re-authentication it MUST be greater than before. The server also sends a random nonce, AT_NONCE_S, and the peer's MAC is calculated over it. Both sides SHOULD have an upper limit on successive fast re-authentications before a full one is required.

Either side may fall back to full authentication. If the server does not recognise the fast re-authentication identity, it asks for a full authentication instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Showing your full ID takes a while. After doing it once, you get a quick one-time ticket that lets you in again fast, and a counter makes sure the same ticket is never used twice.

sections.title: Key Generation
sections.content:
On full authentication a Master Key is derived as MK = SHA1(Identity|IK|CK). It seeds a pseudo-random function based on FIPS 186-2, which produces the Transient EAP Keys that protect EAP-AKA packets (K_encr of 128 bits and K_aut of 128 bits), a Master Session Key (MSK) of 64 bytes for link layer security, and an Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) of 64 bytes for other purposes.

On fast re-authentication the same K_encr and K_aut MUST be used, but a new MSK and EMSK MUST be derived from the original MK and the new values (identity, counter and NONCE_S). The first 32 bytes of the MSK can be used as the Pairwise Master Key for IEEE 802.11i.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared secret is stirred together with your identity to make a set of different keys, each used for one job, so learning one does not give away the others.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
EAP-AKA provides mutual authentication with the EAP server, but not with a separate authenticator, because it does not provide channel bindings. Its effective key strength is 128 bits. Since AKA is not a password protocol, it is not vulnerable to dictionary attacks. AT_MAC, AT_IV, AT_ENCR_DATA and AT_COUNTER provide integrity, replay protection and confidentiality for requests and responses.

There are limits. EAP-AKA/Identity messages cannot be protected by AT_MAC because keys do not yet exist, though AT_CHECKCODE can optionally protect that exchange. EAP-Success, EAP-Failure and Notification packets are not protected, so on insecure networks they could be spoofed for denial of service. EAP method negotiation is not protected, so downgrading attacks may be possible, and there is no ciphersuite or version negotiation.

A malicious peer could flood the Authentication Centre with requests, so servers SHOULD limit their traffic towards it. Identity privacy depends on the pseudonym being kept reliably, otherwise the permanent identity is sent in the clear.
sections.plainLanguage: The card and the network check each other well, but the network cannot prove which door you walked through, and a few plain-text messages could be faked by a bully.

messages.label: EAP-Request/AKA-Challenge
messages.note: AT_RAND, AT_AUTN, AT_MAC. The server has run the AKA algorithms.

messages.label: EAP-Response/AKA-Challenge
messages.note: AT_RES, AT_MAC. The peer has verified AUTN and MAC.

messages.label: EAP-Success
messages.note: The server checked RES and MAC and found them correct.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: 1 for EAP requests, 2 for EAP responses.

fields.desc: Message subtype, defined in Section 11 of the RFC.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved field of the EAP-AKA header.

items.title: Permanent
items.text: Based on the IMSI; full authentication only.

items.title: Pseudonym
items.text: Issued by the server for identity privacy; full authentication only.

items.title: Fast re-authentication
items.text: One-time identity; used only on fast re-authentication.
